candidates.mediaTitle: The winning regions appear to have powerful structural momentum.
candidates.reality: The recent leader won again. Momentum can persist—and successful continuation is what makes extrapolation emotionally sticky. The danger is assuming that one successful rule will remain reliable in the next regime.
candidates.lesson: Continuation is not evidence of certainty. A process can acknowledge momentum without concentrating an investor’s entire decision on the belief that yesterday’s leader must remain tomorrow’s winner.

candidates.mediaTitle: U.S. leadership feels validated by earnings, AI enthusiasm and easing-rate expectations.
candidates.reality: The recent leader stayed on top. This round rewards the obvious choice, reminding players that performance chasing is seductive because it does work in some periods—not because it is consistently dependable.
candidates.lesson: The correct lesson is not “avoid winners.” It is “do not convert a plausible continuation into a certainty or an all-in allocation.”

candidates.mediaTitle: Records, rising confidence and years of strong returns make risk feel unusually manageable.
candidates.reality: Every basket lost money. The five-year leader fell to last place, while the “winner” was merely the region that lost the least. A ranking game can conceal the more important question: whether all risky assets are exposed to the same shock.
candidates.lesson: When optimism is strongest, investors can mistake a relative ranking for an absolute margin of safety. Diversification cannot eliminate a global drawdown, but it can reduce dependence on the most crowded narrative.

candidates.mediaTitle: Strong trailing returns encourage forecasts of another positive year.
candidates.reality: All four baskets declined. The recent leader did not win; the least-bad result came from a different region. Forecasts framed around another year of gains could not neutralise inflation, rate and valuation shocks.
candidates.lesson: A bullish consensus can be reasonable and still be wrong. Risk control begins by asking what happens if the shared premise fails, not by finding one more headline that confirms it.

candidates.mediaTitle: India is framed as fragile while developed-market leadership appears safer.
candidates.reality: The trailing laggard became the next-year winner. The negative narrative described genuine vulnerabilities, but prices and future returns did not wait for the story to become comfortable.
candidates.lesson: An unloved market can remain weak—or reprice sharply before the headlines improve. Contrarian investing is not automatically correct, but avoiding a region solely because its recent story feels frightening can be costly.

candidates.reality: EM ex India moved from the trailing laggard to the next-year winner, while the trailing leader finished last. A highly plausible U.S.-centric story did not identify the strongest regional return.
candidates.lesson: Forecast confidence is often highest when the historical evidence looks clean. That is when a diversified allocation is most valuable: it owns outcomes the dominant narrative may be discounting.

candidates.mediaTitle: India and emerging markets have delivered the most compelling multi-year wealth story.
candidates.reality: The five-year leader became the next-year laggard. The optimistic headlines were not irrational—they were anchored in a powerful run—but they encouraged investors to project a mature trend forward.
candidates.lesson: A long winning history can increase both confidence and embedded expectations. The more popular the story, the more important it becomes to separate business fundamentals from the return already captured in price.

candidates.reality: The two-year leader finished last. The recovery headlines captured real economic strength, yet the next market return was shaped by policy, valuation and sector-specific developments that trailing performance could not summarise.
candidates.lesson: Economic momentum and equity returns are related—but not interchangeable. Markets price expectations, and a strong macro story can coexist with disappointing subsequent returns.

candidates.reality: The trailing leader remained strong but did not finish first. EM ex India took the top spot. This is a subtler failure than a crash: the popular market can perform well while another region performs much better.
candidates.lesson: Opportunity cost is hard to predict. Diversification is not only protection from losses; it also provides exposure to leadership that arrives outside the market receiving the most attention.

candidates.mediaTitle: A difficult year leaves investors expecting instability to dominate again.
candidates.patternLabel: Fear did not pick the winner
candidates.reality: All four baskets rose, but the five-year leader did not lead the rebound. The gloomy environment was understandable; it was not sufficient to rank the following year’s regional returns.
candidates.lesson: After a difficult period, fear can make cash feel like the only rational forecast. Yet recovery may begin before uncertainty is resolved—and its geographic leadership may be different from the previous cycle.

candidates.mediaTitle: Historic losses make another year of danger feel more probable than a violent recovery.
candidates.reality: The trailing laggard became the winner and more than doubled. The headlines accurately described the damage investors had just experienced; they could not tell participants how much bad news was already reflected in prices.
candidates.lesson: The point is not to buy every collapse blindly. It is to recognise that the emotional evidence is strongest near extremes, exactly when forward returns may stop resembling the recent past.

candidates.mediaTitle: Recession expectations and repeated market declines dominate the outlook.
candidates.reality: All four baskets advanced. The recent leader did not necessarily provide a clean forecasting edge, and the fearful consensus did not prevent a strong recovery in risk assets.
candidates.lesson: Macro forecasts can be thoughtful and still fail as market-timing tools. Asset prices respond to the gap between expectations and outcomes—not simply to whether the news is good or bad.
